question: What is Quarkus and how does it differ from Spring Boot?
answer:
Quarkus is a Kubernetes-native Java framework optimised for GraalVM native compilation and fast startup. Key differences from Spring Boot:

  • Build-time processing — much configuration and classpath scanning happens at build time, not runtime.
  • Lower memory footprint — especially in native mode (tens of MB vs hundreds).
  • Faster startup — JVM mode is fast; native mode starts in milliseconds.
  • Reactive-first — built on Vert.x and RESTEasy Reactive; imperative style also supported.
  • Extensions — modular add-ons (like Boot starters) for Hibernate, Kafka, Redis, etc.

Both use CDI-style dependency injection; Quarkus targets cloud/serverless, Spring Boot has the larger enterprise ecosystem.
tip: Quarkus doesn't replace Spring knowledge — many concepts (JPA, REST, CDI) transfer directly.
deep:
Why build-time matters

Spring discovers beans at runtime via classpath scanning — flexible but slow and memory-heavy. Quarkus moves reflection, proxy generation, and config resolution to the build phase, producing a leaner runtime artifact.

When to pick Quarkus

  • Serverless / scale-to-zero (Lambda, Knative)
  • Kubernetes with many small pods
  • Microservices where startup time and memory cost matter

When Spring Boot still wins

  • Large existing Spring codebases
  • Broad third-party integration needs
  • Teams already invested in Spring ecosystem

How to say it in an interview

“Quarkus is a cloud-native Java stack optimised for fast startup and low memory via build-time augmentation and optional native compilation. I'd pick it for serverless or dense K8s deployments; Spring Boot for large enterprise monoliths with deep Spring integration needs.”
revise:
Quarkus = **Kubernetes-native Java** framework tuned for GraalVM native + fast startup.
• **Build-time processing**: scanning/wiring done at build, not runtime → less startup work.
• **Low memory + ms startup** (native ~tens of MB), reactive-first on `Vert.x`.
• **Extensions** = Boot-starter equivalents; CDI-style DI throughout.
• **Interview tip**: JPA/REST/CDI knowledge transfers directly — Quarkus targets cloud/serverless, Boot has the bigger ecosystem.

question: What is Quarkus native compilation and GraalVM?
answer:
GraalVM Native Image compiles Java bytecode ahead-of-time (AOT) into a standalone native binary — no JVM needed at runtime. Benefits: ~10ms startup, ~20–50MB RSS, instant scale-up.

Tradeoffs: longer build times, no dynamic class loading at runtime, reflection must be declared (Quarkus handles most via build-time analysis). Build with ./mvnw package -Pnative.

Quarkus JVM mode is already fast — native is for extreme startup/memory requirements.
tip: Native compilation fails if code uses unregistered reflection — Quarkus extensions pre-configure this for supported libraries.
code: ./mvnw package -Pnative -Dquarkus.native.container-build=true
revise:
**GraalVM Native Image** = AOT-compile bytecode into a standalone binary, no JVM at runtime.
• **Wins**: ~10ms startup, ~20–50MB RSS, instant scale-up.
• **Costs**: slow builds, no dynamic classloading, reflection must be **declared**.
• Build with `./mvnw package -Pnative`.
• **Interview tip**: JVM mode is already fast — go native only for extreme startup/memory needs (serverless, scale-to-zero).

question: How does dependency injection work in Quarkus?
answer:
Quarkus uses CDI (Contexts and Dependency Injection) — the Jakarta EE standard. Inject dependencies with @Inject on fields, constructors, or methods.

Bean scopes: @ApplicationScoped (singleton), @RequestScoped, @Dependent. Define beans with @ApplicationScoped on the class — no @Component equivalent needed.

Quarkus resolves the dependency graph at build time, eliminating runtime CDI container overhead.
tip: Constructor injection is preferred — makes dependencies explicit and eases testing.
revise:
Quarkus DI = **CDI** (Jakarta standard), resolved at **build time** (no runtime container overhead).
• Inject with `@Inject` (field/constructor/method).
• **Scopes**: `@ApplicationScoped` (singleton), `@RequestScoped`, `@Dependent`.
• Declare a bean by putting a scope annotation on the class — no `@Component`.
• **Interview tip**: prefer constructor injection — explicit deps, easier testing.

question: How do you create REST endpoints in Quarkus?
answer:
Use JAX-RS annotations via RESTEasy Reactive (default) or RESTEasy Classic:

  • @Path — base URI
  • @GET, @POST, @PUT, @DELETE
  • @PathParam, @QueryParam, @HeaderParam
  • @Produces / @Consumes — content types

Return types can be synchronous or Uni<T> / Multi<T> for reactive endpoints.
tip: RESTEasy Reactive runs on the Vert.x event loop — blocking calls on the event loop thread will stall the server.
revise:
REST via **JAX-RS** on RESTEasy Reactive (default).
• `@Path` (base URI) + `@GET/@POST/@PUT/@DELETE`.
• Params: `@PathParam`, `@QueryParam`, `@HeaderParam`; `@Produces`/`@Consumes` for content types.
• Return sync objects **or** `Uni<T>`/`Multi<T>` for reactive.
• **Interview tip**: RESTEasy Reactive runs on the Vert.x event loop — a blocking call there stalls the whole server (mark it `@Blocking`).

question: What are Uni and Multi in Quarkus?
answer:
Quarkus uses Mutiny for reactive programming:

  • Uni<T> — emits 0 or 1 item (like a Promise/Single). Use for single async results.
  • Multi<T> — emits 0 to N items (like a Stream). Use for event streams or paginated results.

Composable with .onItem().transform(), .onFailure().recover(), .combine(). Non-blocking I/O on the Vert.x event loop.
tip: Mark blocking work with @Blocking or @RunOnVirtualThread (Java 21+) so it doesn't block the event loop.
revise:
Reactive types come from **Mutiny**.
• **`Uni<T>`** = 0 or 1 item (Promise/Single) — a single async result.
• **`Multi<T>`** = 0..N items (Stream) — event streams / pagination.
• Compose: `.onItem().transform()`, `.onFailure().recover()`, `.combine()`.
• **Interview tip**: wrap blocking work in `@Blocking` or `@RunOnVirtualThread` (Java 21+) so it never blocks the event loop.

question: What is Hibernate Panache?
answer:
Panache is Quarkus's simplified ORM layer on top of Hibernate ORM. Two styles:

  • Active Record — entity extends PanacheEntity; call Person.findById(1) directly on the entity.
  • Repository — entity is a plain JPA class; repository extends PanacheRepository<Person>.

Provides concise query methods, pagination, and integrates with reactive PostgreSQL drivers.
tip: Repository pattern is preferred in larger apps — keeps persistence logic out of domain entities.
revise:
**Panache** = Quarkus's thin, ergonomic layer over Hibernate ORM.
• **Active Record**: entity extends `PanacheEntity` → `Person.findById(1)` on the entity itself.
• **Repository**: plain JPA entity + `PanacheRepository<Person>`.
• Gives concise queries + pagination; works with reactive drivers.
• **Interview tip**: prefer the Repository style in larger apps — keeps persistence logic out of domain entities.

question: How does configuration work in Quarkus?
answer:
Config via application.properties or application.yaml. Inject with @ConfigProperty:

Supports profiles (%dev, %prod), environment variables (automatic mapping), and type-safe config interfaces with @ConfigMapping.

External config via env vars is the standard for containers — no config baked into the image.
tip: QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL env var maps to quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url automatically.
revise:
Config via `application.properties`/`.yaml`, injected with `@ConfigProperty`.
• **Profiles** with `%dev`/`%prod` prefixes.
• **Env vars** map automatically (`QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL` → `quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url`).
• Type-safe groups via `@ConfigMapping`.
• **Interview tip**: in containers, externalise everything through env vars — never bake config into the image.

question: What is Quarkus dev mode?
answer:
Run with ./mvnw quarkus:dev for a development experience with:

  • Live reload — code changes picked up without restart.
  • Dev UI — browser dashboard at /q/dev for config, extensions, continuous testing.
  • H2 dev services — auto-starts a test database if no datasource configured.
  • Test continuous testing — tests re-run on file save.
tip: Dev mode is dramatically faster iteration than traditional Java redeploy cycles.
code: ./mvnw quarkus:dev
revise:
`./mvnw quarkus:dev` = fast inner-loop.
• **Live reload** — code changes picked up with no restart.
• **Dev UI** at `/q/dev` (config, extensions, continuous testing).
• **Dev Services** auto-start a DB/Kafka if none configured.
• **Continuous testing** re-runs tests on save.
• **Interview tip**: this loop is the headline reason Quarkus *feels* faster than classic Java redeploy cycles.

question: What are Quarkus extensions?
answer:
Extensions are modular add-ons that bring capabilities and auto-configuration — analogous to Spring Boot starters. Add via CLI or pom.xml:

quarkus extension add hibernate-orm-panache jdbc-postgresql smallrye-openapi

Each extension contributes build steps, runtime config, and dev services. Only included extensions are in the final binary — no bloat from unused features.
tip: Browse extensions at quarkus.io/extensions — over 300 available.
code:
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-hibernate-orm-panache</artifactId>
</dependency>
revise:
**Extensions** = modular add-ons (build steps + runtime config + dev services), like Boot starters.
• Add via `quarkus extension add ...` or `pom.xml`.
• Only included extensions land in the final binary → **no bloat**.
• 300+ available (Hibernate, Kafka, Redis, OIDC...).
• **Interview tip**: each extension does build-time analysis so native + fast startup 'just work' for supported libs.

question: Health checks and metrics in Quarkus.
answer:
SmallRye Health — /q/health (aggregated), /q/health/live (liveness), /q/health/ready (readiness). Implement custom checks with @Readiness / @Liveness on HealthCheck.

SmallRye Metrics — MicroProfile Metrics at /q/metrics. Annotate with @Counted, @Timed. Integrates with Prometheus via Micrometer.
tip: Kubernetes uses liveness to restart pods and readiness to route traffic — implement both correctly.
revise:
K8s-ready observability out of the box.
• **SmallRye Health**: `/q/health/live` (restart) + `/q/health/ready` (route traffic); custom `@Liveness`/`@Readiness` checks.
• **Metrics** at `/q/metrics` (`@Counted`, `@Timed`), Prometheus via Micrometer.
• **Interview tip**: implement liveness AND readiness — K8s uses liveness to restart pods and readiness to decide when to send traffic.

question: How do you secure REST endpoints in Quarkus?
answer:
Quarkus Security with extensions:

  • quarkus-oidc — OpenID Connect / OAuth2 integration.
  • quarkus-smallrye-jwt — JWT bearer token validation.
  • @RolesAllowed("admin") — restrict by role.
  • @Authenticated — require any authenticated user.

Configure issuer, client, and JWKS URL in application.properties.
tip: Use OIDC extension for Keycloak/Auth0 integration — it handles token validation and role extraction.
revise:
Secure endpoints with the security extensions.
• **`quarkus-oidc`** — OpenID Connect/OAuth2 (Keycloak, Auth0).
• **`quarkus-smallrye-jwt`** — validate JWT bearer tokens.
• Guards: `@RolesAllowed("admin")`, `@Authenticated`.
• **Interview tip**: OIDC handles token validation + role extraction for you — you just configure issuer/JWKS URL.

question: How do you test Quarkus applications?
answer:
@QuarkusTest — boots the full application in test mode (fast thanks to build-time setup). Use @TestHTTPResource for injected test URLs.

RestAssured for HTTP testing. @InjectMock to replace CDI beans with mocks. Testcontainers for real PostgreSQL/Kafka in integration tests.

Dev services auto-provision databases in dev/test without manual Docker setup.
tip: @QuarkusTest starts faster than @SpringBootTest because Quarkus already did build-time wiring.
revise:
**`@QuarkusTest`** boots the app in test mode — fast thanks to build-time wiring.
• `RestAssured` for HTTP, `@TestHTTPResource` for injected URLs.
• `@InjectMock` swaps CDI beans; **Testcontainers**/Dev Services give a real Postgres/Kafka.
• **Interview tip**: it starts faster than `@SpringBootTest` because Quarkus already did the wiring at build time.

question: Database migrations with Flyway in Quarkus.
answer:
Add quarkus-flyway extension. Place SQL scripts in src/main/resources/db/migration/ named V1__create_orders.sql, V2__add_status.sql.

Flyway runs migrations on startup automatically. Configure with quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=true.
tip: Never modify a migration that's already been applied to production — add a new versioned script instead.
code:
# application.properties
quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=true
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost/orders
revise:
**Flyway** = versioned SQL migrations via `quarkus-flyway`.
• Scripts in `src/main/resources/db/migration/` named `V1__create_orders.sql`, `V2__...`.
• Run on startup (`quarkus.flyway.migrate-at-start=true`).
• **Interview tip**: never edit an already-applied migration — add a new versioned script (Flyway tracks a checksum and will refuse a changed one).

question: How do you schedule tasks in Quarkus?
answer:
Quarkus Scheduler extension — annotate methods with @Scheduled:

  • every = "10s" — fixed interval
  • cron = "0 0 1 * * ?" — cron expression
  • delay = 5 — initial delay

Runs on worker threads by default — safe for blocking operations.
tip: For distributed scheduling across multiple pods, use an external scheduler or Kafka — @Scheduled runs on every instance.
revise:
**`@Scheduled`** (Quarkus Scheduler extension) on a method.
• `every="10s"` (interval), `cron="0 0 1 * * ?"`, `delay=5` (initial).
• Runs on **worker threads** → blocking-safe.
• **Interview tip**: it fires on *every* instance — for one-run-across-the-cluster use an external scheduler, a lock, or Kafka.

question: Caching in Quarkus.
answer:
Add quarkus-cache extension. Annotate methods with @CacheResult(cacheName = "users") to cache return values. @CacheInvalidate evicts entries.

Backends: Caffeine (in-memory, default) or Redis (quarkus-redis-cache) for distributed caching across pods.
tip: Cache keys are derived from method parameters by default — customise with @CacheKey on specific params.
revise:
Method-level caching via `quarkus-cache`.
• `@CacheResult(cacheName="users")` caches the return; `@CacheInvalidate` evicts.
• **Caffeine** in-memory by default; **Redis** for shared cache across pods.
• Key derived from method params; override with `@CacheKey`.
• **Interview tip**: in-memory cache doesn't share across pods — reach for Redis once you scale horizontally.

question: How does Quarkus generate OpenAPI documentation?
answer:
Add quarkus-smallrye-openapi. Scans JAX-RS endpoints and generates an OpenAPI 3 spec automatically.

Access at /q/openapi (JSON/YAML). Swagger UI at /q/swagger-ui. Enrich with @Operation, @APIResponse, @Schema annotations.
tip: OpenAPI spec is generated at build time in Quarkus — no runtime scanning overhead.
revise:
`quarkus-smallrye-openapi` auto-generates an **OpenAPI 3** spec from JAX-RS endpoints.
• Spec at `/q/openapi`, Swagger UI at `/q/swagger-ui`.
• Enrich with `@Operation`, `@APIResponse`, `@Schema`.
• **Interview tip**: generated at **build time** in Quarkus — no runtime scanning cost.

question: Global exception handling in Quarkus.
answer:
Implement ExceptionMapper<T extends Exception> — a JAX-RS provider that converts exceptions to HTTP responses:

Annotate with @Provider and implement toResponse(T exception). Quarkus discovers it via CDI.

For validation errors, quarkus-hibernate-validator returns 400 with constraint violation details automatically.
tip: Map business exceptions (OrderNotFoundException) to 404, validation to 400, unknown to 500 without exposing internals.
revise:
Global handling = implement **`ExceptionMapper<T>`** + `@Provider`.
• `toResponse(T e)` turns an exception into an HTTP response; Quarkus discovers it via CDI.
• `quarkus-hibernate-validator` auto-returns 400 with constraint details.
• **Interview tip**: map business exceptions to 404, validation to 400, unknown to 500 — never leak internals/stack traces.

question: Transaction management in Quarkus.
answer:
Use @Transactional on CDI bean methods (from Narayana JTA). Default propagation: REQUIRED — joins existing transaction or creates new one.

Options: rollbackOn, dontRollbackOn, value = TxType.REQUIRES_NEW for independent transactions.

Works with Hibernate Panache — a single @Transactional method can call multiple repository operations atomically.
tip: @Transactional only works on CDI bean methods called through the proxy — not on private methods or self-invocation.
revise:
**`@Transactional`** (Narayana JTA) on a CDI bean method.
• Default propagation **REQUIRED** (join or start a tx); `REQUIRES_NEW` for an independent one; `rollbackOn`/`dontRollbackOn` tune rollback rules.
• Multiple Panache calls in one method = atomic.
• **Interview tip**: only works through the CDI proxy — self-invocation and private methods silently bypass it.

question: How does Quarkus integrate with Kafka?
answer:
Add quarkus-smallrye-reactive-messaging-kafka. Use MicroProfile Reactive Messaging channels:

  • Incoming — @Incoming("orders") on a method consuming messages.
  • Outgoing — @Outgoing("orders") on a method producing messages, or inject @Channel("orders") Emitter<Order>.

Configure broker, serializers, and consumer group in application.properties.
tip: Dev services can spin up a Kafka broker automatically in dev mode — zero local setup.
revise:
Kafka via `quarkus-smallrye-reactive-messaging-kafka` (MicroProfile Reactive Messaging).
• **`@Incoming("orders")`** consumes; **`@Outgoing("orders")`** produces, or inject `@Channel Emitter<Order>`.
• Broker/serializers/consumer-group in config.
• **Interview tip**: Dev Services spins up a Kafka broker automatically in dev — zero local setup.

question: Blocking vs reactive endpoints — when to use which?
answer:
Reactive (Uni/Multi) — non-blocking I/O on the event loop. Best for high-concurrency I/O (many simultaneous requests, reactive DB drivers).

Blocking (imperative) — traditional synchronous code. Use @Blocking or run on a worker thread pool. Fine for most CRUD apps.

Virtual threads (Java 21+) — @RunOnVirtualThread gives blocking-style code with reactive-scale concurrency.
tip: Don't prematurely optimise for reactive — imperative Quarkus on JVM is already very fast for typical REST APIs.
revise:
Pick the execution model per workload.
• **Reactive** (`Uni`/`Multi`): non-blocking on the event loop → best for high-concurrency I/O + reactive DB drivers.
• **Blocking**: plain imperative; use `@Blocking`/worker thread — fine for typical CRUD.
• **Virtual threads** (`@RunOnVirtualThread`, Java 21+): blocking style, reactive-scale concurrency.
• **Interview tip**: don't reach for reactive prematurely — imperative Quarkus on the JVM is already very fast.

question: What are Quarkus profiles?
answer:
Profiles activate environment-specific configuration. Set via quarkus.profile=dev or %prod prefix in properties:

%dev.quarkus.log.level=DEBUG
%prod.quarkus.log.level=WARN

Default profiles: dev, test, prod. Custom profiles supported. Beans can be profile-specific with @IfBuildProfile("dev").
tip: In Kubernetes, set QUARKUS_PROFILE=prod — never ship dev profile config to production.
code:
%dev.quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:h2:mem:test
%prod.quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=${DATABASE_URL}
revise:
**Profiles** activate environment-specific config.
• Built-in `dev`/`test`/`prod`; select via `quarkus.profile` or `%prod.` prefix.
• e.g. `%dev.quarkus.log.level=DEBUG`.
• Profile-specific beans: `@IfBuildProfile("dev")`.
• **Interview tip**: set `QUARKUS_PROFILE=prod` in K8s — never ship dev config to production.

question: Quarkus and Kubernetes — what makes it cloud-native?
answer:
Quarkus generates Kubernetes manifests via extensions (quarkus-kubernetes, quarkus-openshift). Auto-configures:

  • Health probes pointing to /q/health/ready and /q/health/live
  • Resource limits based on native vs JVM mode
  • Service discovery and config maps
  • Container image via quarkus-container-image-docker

Fast startup + low memory = higher pod density and faster autoscaling.
tip: quarkus.kubernetes.deploy=true deploys directly from Maven in dev — useful for quick iteration on OpenShift/K8s.
code: ./mvnw package -Dquarkus.container-image.build=true
revise:
Cloud-native = fast startup + low memory + generated manifests.
• `quarkus-kubernetes`/`-openshift` emit YAML wired to `/q/health/*` probes, resource limits, config maps.
• Container image via `quarkus-container-image-docker`.
• Low RSS + ms startup → higher pod density + faster autoscaling.
• **Interview tip**: `quarkus.kubernetes.deploy=true` deploys straight from Maven — handy for quick K8s/OpenShift iteration.
